why403: The store refused it. For the paths this service is NOT supposed to reach that is the read-only policy working and not a fault — the identity it holds is bound to two read paths and nothing else.
why404: No such path in the store. For a KV version 2 secret that usually means the engine is mounted somewhere else, or the secret has not been written yet.
why400: The store rejected the request itself. A KV version 1 engine answers this to a version 2 path, which is the usual cause.
whyEnoent: There is no such file. On a DEVELOPMENT-mode service that is ordinary: nothing is persisted, so the key-encryption key is never read and the file it names need not exist. In product mode this is a service that would not start.
whyEacces: The file is there and this process may not read it. Check the ownership of the mount rather than the path.
whyTimeout: The store did not answer inside keys.storeProbeTimeoutMs. That bounds one probe and not the page, so the others below were still asked.
whySdk: The SDK for this provider is not installed. It is deliberately not a dependency of this service — it is a mock first, and five cloud SDKs nobody uses would be carried by every install — so the message above names the package to install.
whatIs: This page is where this service’s two primordial secrets come from, whether it actually got them, and what the store at the other end is doing. It reads them and never writes one: the key-encryption key is generated by nobody here, and neither is the database password.
whatThree: Three pages touch this subject and they answer three questions.
whatConfig: , under Server configuration, holds the keys.* settings and says what this service is set up to do.
whatEncryption: says what is sealed and with what. This one says what is at the other end of that: a file’s mode and mtime, or a store’s seal state, its version, its leader, the certificate this service proves itself with and when that expires, what its policy actually grants, and every version of the secret the store has kept. All of that can be broken while every settings row is right.
whatNoControl: No secret value appears here and there is no control on this page. No reveal, no rotate, no test-read. A reveal is the end of the key. A rotate would destroy everything sealed under it, because this service has no re-sealing pass — which is exactly why the key is written once. And a test-read would be this console causing the one thing the whole design avoids: the key in this process’s memory because somebody opened a page. Every probe below reads METADATA — a stat, a sys endpoint, a version history, a DescribeSecret — and not one of them fetches a stored value.
whatTitle: What this page is, and the three controls it deliberately has not got
halfFail: Half the probes on this page are supposed to fail, and a 403 is usually the good news. The identity this service holds in a secret store is bound to two read paths and nothing else — it cannot write its own key, cannot rotate it out from under the data sealed with it, and cannot plant one of its own — so a refusal against anything else is the policy working. A page that hid those refusals would be hiding the evidence for the claim.
eachProbe: Each probe is run, timed and caught separately, bounded by keys.storeProbeTimeoutMs at {ms}ms, and they run in parallel: a store that is entirely unreachable costs that bound once rather than once per question asked of it.
halfFailTitle: Why a failed probe here is not the same as a failed probe anywhere else
unusedDev: This service is in development mode and is not persisting signing keys, so it has never asked for the key-encryption key. Everything below about that secret describes what would happen, and the ordinary unavailable rows on this page are this service correctly not needing something.
unusedSigning: Signing keys are generated on every start and held in memory here, which is what makes this service disposable. global.mode=product, or keys.source=persisted, is what makes the key real — and in product mode a key that cannot be read is a service that does not start.
unusedTitle: Nothing here is load-bearing on this service, yet
noProvider: No provider is configured, so this service does not read it from a store. {setting} selects one.
noProviderTitle: Not read from a secret store
readOkMemory: This process holds the value in memory and nothing wrote it to disk. It is not on this page, in the JSON behind it, or in any log line this service has ever emitted.
notRead: This process has not read it. That is not by itself a fault: a secret is read when something needs it, and in development mode on a memory store nothing does. It does mean nothing below has been proved by use.
fieldWhy: Which member is taken when what is stored is a JSON object. A stored value that is not JSON is taken whole. Set by {setting}.
sharedLocation: This secret names no location, so it is read from wherever the key-encryption key is and the field above is what tells the two apart inside one value. That is the arrangement a deployment with one mounted file or one cloud secret is already in. If what is there turns out NOT to be a JSON object, reading this secret is REFUSED rather than handing that key to a database.
namesLocation: It names its own location in {setting}.
whatItIsTitle: What it is, and what happens without it
storeSays: What the store says about this secret
noStores: Neither secret is read from a store, so there is none to report on.
perStore: One block per store and not per secret: two secrets kept in one place share everything below, and asking the same store twice whether it is sealed would be this page inventing a disagreement it then has to draw.
nothingPublished: This provider publishes nothing about the store itself beyond what is already on the secret above — a cloud secret manager is an endpoint and an access policy, and everything it will say is said about the secret.
